# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
**Summary as I read it:** using the Halden microdata, Varga and Holm document four problems:
- **Attrition:** withdrawals happened mostly *after* the schedule began, for workload reasons.
- **Output:** the manager-reported index runs 3.8 points above organisations' own records.
- **Hours:** actual hours fell about 14%, not the scheduled 20%.
- **Revenue:** the comparison was nominal.

Correcting output and hours cuts the per-hour gain from 23.4% to 10.8% in a 17-organisation subset. They then argue that this residual is novelty, dismiss Varden's meetings analysis, and conclude that per-hour gains from reduced hours are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

Sections 1–5 are good work and should carry real weight. Sections 6–8 overshoot. Having corrected Halden's inflation, the comment lands on the opposite failure, as in the "failures come in pairs" item of the How We Work note. It closes a question its own evidence leaves open, and dismisses the strongest counter-evidence.

## What the comment earns

- **The attrition finding is the most important new fact.** The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show that 7 of 9 withdrew after the schedule began, and 6 gave workload or output as the reason. That is a misreport, not just a limitation, and it confirms the survivor concern I raised about the working paper.
- **The manager vs records comparison is persuasive.** In 19 of 23 organisations the manager index was higher. A sign test on that split gives p ≈ 0.003. The 3.8-point gap is systematic.
- **The hours correction is right in direction and roughly in size.** It matches Varden's case-processing result: a 13% cut in actual hours against 20% scheduled.
- **The arithmetic checks out.** The Table 2 rows give 23.4, 18.9, 14.6 and 10.8. The hours falls of −14.1% and −13.9% are correct, and the real revenue change is 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ −2.6%.
- **The sectoral point (§5) is well supported.** Three retail organisations with records show −11.2%, which lines up with Varden's −11.4% in its counter stratum.

## Where it overreaches

**1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own analysis.** Section 6 says "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." The Data Note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the abstract and conclusion state that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" for reduced-hours schemes *in general*. A 10.8% residual that the authors cannot explain is an open question, not a demonstrated zero. They also give no confidence interval for that residual. The defensible conclusion is that the Halden gain shrinks to about 11% after correction, and that its durability is unknown.

**2. It cites half of Varden.** The counter stratum is called "the most reliable finding in the literature." The case-processing stratum of the same randomised trial goes unmentioned. That stratum found +12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4), and it was built to avoid every problem the comment raises:
- output from administrative records;
- hours from timesheets;
- a randomised control group;
- no reported attrition;
- nine months' duration.

By the comment's own standards it is at least as reliable as the counter stratum. With 14 offices rather than 10 and a narrower interval, it is arguably more precise. Its result is close to the comment's corrected Halden figure. Two independent estimates of roughly 11–12% per actual hour in non-coverage work are the opposite of "entirely an artifact."

**3. The novelty argument is a hypothesis stated as a finding.**
- The extrapolation is arithmetically off and methodologically weak. A linear decline from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 at month 6 reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." A straight line through two points is also no basis for predicting a plateau or a return to zero.
- Energy is not output. The link from self-reported energy to per-hour output is asserted, not shown.
- Varden's case-processing gain was still present at month 9, which is near or beyond the comment's own projected return to baseline. That is a different setting and doesn't settle the matter, but it is the only longer-run controlled data available and it points the other way.
- "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" is fair. But not having proven durability is not the same as having shown an artifact.

**4. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- The comment says the seven offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known." In fact they are the *entire* treated case-processing stratum, which was defined before randomisation, not a selected subgroup.
- Varden says the meetings data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- Varden already said what the comment says: not registered, n = 7, "cannot establish a mechanism." It has registered a confirmatory test.

The comment is attacking a stronger claim than the one Varden made. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is right, and Varden agrees. "Post hoc account fitted to a subgroup" is inaccurate.

**5. A missing alternative.** The comment offers three explanations for the residual: measurement, selection and novelty. It leaves out **reorganisation**, meaning fewer meetings, simpler approvals and less low-value reporting. Halden's managers reported these changes, and Varden measured meetings. My rough calculation from the Varden figures suggested meeting cuts could explain most of the case-processing per-hour gain. If that holds, the residual is neither novelty nor rest. It is real, structural and probably fairly durable, although meetings can creep back. That would also mean the gain could be had without cutting hours. This is a live, testable line, and Varden's 24-month follow-up can tell it apart from novelty.

## Internal inconsistencies to fix

- **The hours decomposition (§3) doesn't add up.** Baseline is 40.3 hours a week, roughly 8.06 a day. Four days at +0.7 hours each plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4–36.6 hours, not 34.6. The figures work if the extension is about +0.7 hours *per week*, not per day. As written, one of the numbers is wrong.
- **The abstract says "correcting the first three"** problems, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never corrected, and probably can't be without outcome data for the organisations that withdrew. The abstract should say two.
- **"Account for most of the reported gain."** The corrections take the figure from 23.4% to 10.8%, so they account for about 54% of it. "Most" is technically true, but it sits awkwardly next to "entirely."

## Smaller points

- **Record-based output may have its own bias.** "Billable hours delivered" is partly an *hours* measure. Fewer hours worked mechanically means fewer hours billed, which pushes the record-based index down for reasons unrelated to productivity. It would help to know how many of the 23 used it.
- **The record subsets are self-selected** (23, 27 and 17 organisations), as the Data Note concedes. The direction of that bias is unclear: organisations with time tracking may be better-run.
- **Revenue.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue; producer or sector prices would be better. The direction of the correction is right. I raised the same point conditionally on the working paper.
- **The recommendations in §8 are sound.** In particular, "analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw."

## Where the three documents leave things

- **Settled:**
  - Uncontrolled pilots using scheduled hours and manager ratings overstate per-hour gains roughly twofold.
  - In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output and service.
  - Halden misreported its attrition.
- **Supported but not settled:** a gain of roughly 11–12% per actual hour in backlog and knowledge work, from two independent sources: one randomised, one corrected observational.
- **Open:** whether that gain lasts, and how much comes from reorganisation versus rest versus novelty. Varden's 24-month follow-up is the key test. Ideally it would add a meetings-only arm.

I can draft a short reply to the comment along these lines, or a reconciliation table setting the Halden, corrected-Halden and Varden estimates side by side with what each controls for.
